## 1. Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
- **2026-11-17** · bioinformatics
- why: Presents a fast, structure-free ML model for binding affinity prediction using only sequence and SMILES, directly advancing computational screening.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.15.766769
- abstract: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

## 2. On improving experimental binding affinity predictions with synthetic data
- **2026-11-20** · molecular biology
- why: Shows that synthetic data from free energy perturbation improves binding affinity predictions, a key advance for ML in drug discovery.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.02.708607
- abstract: The success of deep learning binding affinity prediction models depends critically on expanding experimental data with reliable synthetic data. We extend the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR) with {approx}80K absolute free energy perturbation (AFEP) calculations and present two distinct data splits, SAIR-FEP and SAIR-OOD (out-of-distribution), to simulate realistic drug discovery scenarios. We compare sequence-based proteochemometric (PCM) models and state-of-the-art, structure-based deep learning models and demonstrate that PCM models can be enhanced by physics-based descriptors in the cross-target hit-identification setting. While structure-based deep learning methods capture finer geometric detail, their performance is highly sensitive to the input structure. By filtering for high-confidence, co-folded complexes, we show that the performance improves predictably, whereas training on all complexes blindly limits performance gains. Finally, using the SAIR-OOD split, we demonstrate that simultaneous training on synthetic and experimental data improves performance on publicly available, experimental benchmarks. For the OpenBind benchmark, our models yield the lowest root mean squared errors and a 1.85x improvement of Spearman ranking correlation when compared to the original AEVPLIG model training on experimental data alone. These results provide a clear strategy for using synthetic data to advance experimental binding affinity predictions.

## 3. Lacuna: Cryptic Binding Pocket Discovery via Conformational Ensemble Analysis
- **2026-11-16** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a tool for cryptic pocket discovery from conformational ensembles, enabling targeting of previously undruggable sites.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.14.744956
- abstract: Lacuna, an open-source Python tool for discovering cryptic binding pockets: sites that are absent or too small to detect in the unbound structure of a protein, RNA or DNA and open only during conformational fluctuation. Most binding-site predictors score a single static structure, the very structure in which a cryptic site is invisible. Lacuna generates a conformational ensemble from any input structure, detects pockets independently in every conformer, clusters the detections into persistent sites, and ranks those sites with a model fitted on within-structure pairs. Ensemble generation is pluggable: normal mode analysis (NMA) by default, with implicit-solvent molecular dynamics, Boltz-2 diffusion sampling or a user-supplied ensemble as alternatives. On the designated test fold of CryptoBench, all 222 structures of which are scored, the zero-dependency default recovers the cryptic site for 59.9% of structures in its top five predictions, and it recovers 69% on the PocketMiner set, 41% on a curated set of literature apo/holo pairs and 89% of structures in the already-open COACH420 set. On that test fold, ordering the candidate set with the fitted ranker rather than the analytic rule it replaced accounts for a gain of 27.5 points (95% CI +21.2 to +33.8), the largest single effect measured here. An optional protein-language-model (PLM) ranker reaches 66.1% on a 180-structure subset of that fold, and pooling the geometric detector with an optional learned surface detector raises top-five recovery to 73.9% and the fraction of structures in which the site is found at all to 86.4% in a separate held-out evaluation at five conformers (184 structures; both optional configurations measured with version 1.4.0). A new per-residue cryptic-site propensity reaches AUROC 0.766 and AUPRC 0.340 on the same test fold (231 targets), against 0.249 for the same scorer on the input structure alone, so the ensemble carries information the input does not. RNA and DNA need no extra flags; on RNA sites with no cavity in the input the ensemble raises the fraction found from 44% to 73% (measured with version 1.3.0). With the default NMA backend the pocket report is identical at any thread count and between Windows and Linux on the 40 proteins compared, ensemble generation needs less than half the memory of version 1.4.0 from 1,300 residues up, and the full pipeline is 7% to 30% faster than 1.4.0 on the reference proteins of the repository's speed table. At the default 20 conformers it takes a median of 1.9 seconds per chain on one CPU thread (30 chains of 57 to 676 residues). Outputs include docking-ready Boltz constraints and AutoDock Vina boxes, a per-residue propensity map and the conformer ensemble. Lacuna is MIT licensed, available at https://github.com/mooreneural/lacuna and on PyPI as lacuna-pockets, and runs as a local MCP server for AI assistants and on hosted no-install platforms.

## 4. Conserved Vulnerability, Local Tunability: How Binding Proteins Read Ligand Fluorination
- **2026-11-19** · biophysics
- why: Provides mechanistic insights into how proteins recognize fluorinated ligands, combining structural and thermodynamic data to inform drug design.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.17.767237
- abstract: While rare in nature, fluorinated compounds are ubiquitous in synthetic chemicals ranging from pharmaceuticals to agrochemicals, yet how proteins recognize these anthropogenic molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use three structurally and evolutionarily divergent solute-binding proteins (SBPs) specific for short-chain dicarboxylic acids as a comparative model system to dissect the principles governing protein-fluorocompound recognition. X-ray crystal structures reveal that each SBP uses a distinct binding mode, ranging from backbone-mediated to side-chain-dominated hydrogen bonding. Despite their structural divergence, ITC shows that all three proteins exhibit a conserved vulnerability upon binding perfluorinated ligands: binding affinity drops up to 80-fold, or is abolished, across all three proteins regardless of fold or binding mode. In contrast, sensitivity to partial fluorination is locally tunable, with one protein even binding a fluorinated ligand more tightly than its non-fluorinated counterpart. Using X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and site-directed mutagenesis, we show that aromatic residues positioned near the ligand contribute to this tunability, capable of either penalizing or favoring fluorinated ligands. Together, these findings establish that ligand-fluorination sensitivity reflects a conserved chemical vulnerability layered with locally tunable, structurally encoded selectivity, providing a roadmap for predicting and engineering protein recognition of fluorinated compounds.

## 5. Docking and SPR identify candidate interactions between Apolipoprotein A-I and chemokine receptors
- **2026-11-17** · molecular biology
- why: Combines docking and SPR to identify direct ApoA1-chemokine receptor interactions, providing binding data and a new target hypothesis.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.14.766677
- abstract: Background: Apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1), the main protein component of high-density lipoprotein, suppresses chemokine-driven leukocyte migration. This effect is usually attributed to indirect mechanisms such as cholesterol efflux, changes in lipid rafts, and altered receptor expression. Whether ApoA1 interacts with chemokine receptors directly is not known. Methods: We combined in silico rigid-body docking of AlphaFold-predicted structures (GRAMM-X, with interface analysis by PDBePISA) and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). In SPR experiments, ApoA1 was immobilized on the sensor, and CCR1, CCR5, CX3CR1, CXCR2, and CXCR4 were incorporated into proteoliposomes and injected as analytes. Mock proteoliposomes lacking any receptor served as a negative control. Kinetics were fitted with a 1:1 Langmuir model. Results: Docking predicted favorable interfaces between ApoA1 and all five receptors. CCR1 had the most favorable docking interaction, and CCR5 had the largest predicted interface (3716.7 A;iG -62.8 kcal/mol). Mock proteoliposomes showed no detectable binding to ApoA1, whereas all five receptors bound to ApoA1 in the SPR experiments. The apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) were 3.44x10^-8 M for CXCR4, 3.96x10^-8 M for CXCR2, 5.26x10^-8 M for CCR5, 4.35x10^-7 M for CCR1, and 1.23x10^-6 M for CX3CR1. Conclusions: ApoA1 appears to bind chemokine receptors directly, with the highest apparent affinities for CXCR4, CXCR2, and CCR5. These findings suggest a candidate mechanism, complementary to cholesterol efflux and receptor expression regulation, by which ApoA1 may influence chemokine signaling. However, whether binding alters receptor signaling, internalization, or cell migration remains to be determined.

## 6. Binding Entropy Can Be Predicted by Crystallographic Ensembles
- **2026-11-16** · biophysics
- why: Develops a method to predict binding entropy from crystallographic ensembles, directly improving understanding of protein-ligand thermodynamics.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.01.19.699807
- abstract: Protein-ligand binding is governed by free energy, comprising both enthalpic and entropic contributions. Yet structural interpretations of binding thermodynamics have predominantly focused on enthalpic interactions, largely neglecting entropy because it is difficult to quantify from static structural models. Here, we developed multiconformer ensemble models to analyze high-resolution X-ray crystallography structures and estimate both protein and solvent conformational entropies. These ensemble models successfully predicted experimental binding entropies measured by isothermal titration calorimetry for over 70 protein-ligand pairs across 12 proteins, revealing a strong linear correlation. Protein entropy, estimated using crystallographic order parameters that capture both harmonic and anharmonic motion, correlates linearly with experimental binding entropy. Incorporating resolution-corrected differences in water-molecule counts substantially improves predictions, demonstrating that protein and solvent contributions must be considered jointly. Analysis of water-protein hydrogen bonding networks partially explains entropic differences across complexes. These results establish that crystallographic ensembles can quantify binding entropy, enabling explicit entropic considerations in structure-based studies of molecular recognition for both functional analysis and drug design.

## 7. Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
- **2026-11-17** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a virtual receptor framework that generates realistic peptide binding data for ML training, directly advancing computational peptide design and active learning.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.16.766906
- abstract: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor's ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while highlighting areas for further refinement.

## 8. De Novo Design of Miniprotein Binders Targeting the Leptin-Binding Site of the Leptin Receptor
- **2026-11-18** · biochemistry
- why: Describes de novo computational design of miniprotein binders against the leptin receptor, a first-in-class target for obesity, with high-affinity binding validated experimentally.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.16.766359
- abstract: The leptin receptor (LEPR) regulates appetite, energy balance, glucose homeostasis, and neuroendocrine function and is closely associated with obesity, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Activation of LEPR signaling suppresses appetite and promotes energy expenditure, whereas impaired LEPR signaling and leptin resistance are commonly associated with obesity. Accordingly, modulation of LEPR signaling is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity and related metabolic disorders. In this study, we report the de novo computational design of miniprotein binders targeting the leptin-binding site within the cytokine receptor homology 2 (CRH2) domain of LEPR. Computational screening and biochemical characterization identified the miniprotein binder Mini-19484, which adopted a stable -helical fold and exhibited enhanced resistance to proteolytic degradation. Mini-19484 bound the LEPR CRH2 domain with high affinity, with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 30 nM. Structural analysis of the predicted model and mutagenesis studies revealed that Arg18 of Mini-19484 serves as a critical interaction hotspot for LEPR binding. The predicted binding mode of Mini-19484 differed substantially from that of natural leptin, providing a distinct molecular scaffold for targeting the LEPR CRH2 domain. These findings provide a valuable framework for developing miniprotein-based therapeutics targeting LEPR.

## 9. De novo design of antiviral monobody binders
- **2026-11-16** · biochemistry
- why: Presents a computational pipeline for de novo design of monobody binders against viral antigens, with experimental validation for SARS-CoV-2, relevant to emerging targets.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.12.760042
- abstract: Monobodies (Mobs) are a class of immunoglobulin (Ig)-like proteins that have emerged as promising therapeutic scaffolds for applications ranging from antiviral therapy to cancer treatment. Unlike conventional monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), Mobs can be readily expressed in Escherichia coli at high yields, offering important advantages in overall developability. However, discovering antigen-specific Mobs with high binding affinity traditionally requires screening large, randomized in vitro libraries. To optimize Mob discovery, we developed MobGen, a computational pipeline for de novo design of Mob binders against viral antigens. As a proof of concept, we generated Mobs that bind the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein Receptor Binding Domain (RBD). Subsequent in silico optimization improved production yield, thermal and conformational stability, binding affinity, and antiviral activity, demonstrating a promising approach for rapidly developing antibody-like molecules that target viral entry. These findings highlight MobGen's potential for de novo design of Mobs against emerging viruses with pandemic potential.

## 10. Rational Design of Molecular Glue Degraders Utilizing Endogenous Transient Protein-Protein Interactions
- **2026-11-17** · biochemistry
- why: Introduces a rational design strategy for molecular glues targeting transient protein-protein interactions, with cryo-EM and virtual screening, advancing emerging target modulation.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.16.766899
- abstract: Molecular glues are small molecules that modulate protein activity by inducing or stabilizing protein-protein interactions (PPIs). However, identifying and harnessing endogenous protein pairs amenable to small-molecule-mediated stabilization remains a major challenge in molecular glue development. Here we introduce transient interface pocket-guided molecular glue rational design (TrIP-MGRD), a strategy that shifts compound discovery from empirical screening toward rational, interaction-guided design by exploiting druggable pockets at transient PPI interfaces. Using CDK12 as a model target, we identified DDB1 as an endogenous transient interaction partner and determined the DDB1-CDK12-CCNK complex structure by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Structure-guided virtual screening and medicinal chemistry optimization yielded a molecular glue C432 that stabilized this interaction. Comparison of the ligand-free and C432-bound complexes revealed pre-existing contacts at the transient CDK12-DDB1 interface provides a structural basis for compound-mediated stabilization. Collectively, by integrating endogenous partner identification with interface-guided screening, TrIP-MGRD provides a new framework for target-directed molecular glue discovery.

## 11. BrainRoute integrates machine learning prediction with community-driven verification of blood-brain barrier permeability
- **2026-11-20** · neuroscience
- why: Integrates ML prediction and community verification for BBB permeability, directly aiding CNS drug development.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.19.767839
- abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective barrier that restricts the entry of many therapeutic agents into the brain. The lack of efficient methods for BBB permeability research and data management remains a significant challenge for central nervous system drug-development pipelines. Although BBB permeability data are available from multiple open sources, few platforms integrate these datasets with molecular exploration, predictive tools, and a structured process for community-supported data verification. Here, we present BrainRoute, an open platform for BBB molecular data collection, exploration, prediction, and community-supported verification. BrainRoute provides searchable and filterable molecular records, physicochemical and structural information, source-linked data, single-molecule and batch prediction, and a structured workflow through which users can submit additional evidence for review. The prediction tool model-development cohort contained 7,888 unique molecules, including 5,424 BBB+ and 2,464 BBB- molecules. Six machine-learning classifiers were evaluated using PaDEL descriptors, Morgan fingerprints, frozen ChemBERTa embeddings, and combined feature representations. The three selected models were integrated into the platform as a probability-averaged ensemble. The primary five-fold scaffold-grouped analysis achieved a best mean balanced accuracy of 0.783 {+/-} 0.026. On an independent external set containing 410 non-overlapping molecules, the deployed ensemble achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.659 (95% CI 0.600 - 0.712) and an AUPRC of 0.670 (95% CI 0.583 - 0.752). BrainRoute serves as a platform for exploring BBB-related molecular data and computational predictions while supporting the continued growth and verification of the underlying dataset. BrainRoute is freely accessible online (https://github.com/omicscodeathon/brainroutedb).

## 12. ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
- **2026-11-16** · bioinformatics
- why: Presents a GNN to predict protein flexibility from static structures, advancing ML for structural biology.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.13.766391
- abstract: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals-related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction.

## 13. A Molecular Glue that Regulates Processing of Non-Coding RNAs in Human Cells
- **2026-11-17** · biochemistry
- why: Describes a molecular glue targeting ncRNAs, a novel and undruggable target class.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.14.766697
- abstract: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are a major class of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and essential components of the spliceosome. Chemical tools for perturbing snRNA structure and function are lacking, and ncRNAs have more generally been considered undruggable. Here we use chemical proteomics and cryo-electron microscopy to identify a covalent molecular glue HL-1B that stabilizes binding of the 3'-exonuclease TOE1 to the spliceosome in a catalytically competent state. We show that HL-1B triggers excess 3'-processing of snRNAs in human cells that is tunable by the expression levels of TOE1 and auxiliary splicing regulators like SNRPB2, which, in turn, create synthetic lethality interactions with HL-1B that correlate with the preferential modulation of intermediate exon inclusion splicing events. Our findings reveal a fundamental role for snRNA tail length in regulating spliceosome function and, more generally, a way to target ncRNAs with non-orthosteric small molecules that remodel the interactomes of RNA processing enzymes in cells.

## 14. High-throughput prediction of peptide structural conformations
- **2026-11-17** · bioinformatics
- why: Applies AlphaFold2 for multi-conformation prediction of peptides, relevant to ML for structural biology.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem
- https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.12.03.626727
- abstract: Protein structure prediction via artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) approaches has sparked substantial research interest in structural biology. In recent work, AlphaFold2 (AF2) has been adapted for the prediction of multiple structural conformations, beyond static structures, by using multiple random seeds and subsampling the multiple sequence alignment (MSA). Research applying this specialized approach has focused on regular-sized proteins, while smaller peptides remain underexplored in this context. Here, we report AF2-based multi-conformation prediction and systematic analyses of a set of 557 peptides (10-40 residues in length) with corresponding nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) ensemble coordinates. We found that predicted ensembles varied in similarity to experimental coordinate data, with disulfide-rich peptides bearing somewhat closer resemblance whereas -helical peptides exhibited greater dissimilarity. Distinct correlations involving MSA depth were also observed. These results reveal notable capabilities of AF2-based multi-conformation prediction for peptides but also highlight considerable limitations, emphasizing the need for interpretation discretion and improved multi-conformation prediction approaches.

## 15. Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
- **2026-11-17** · bioengineering
- why: Introduces sparse autoencoders to interpret and manipulate ProteinMPNN, enabling targeted sequence design for improved thermostability.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765161
- abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

## 16. Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
- **2026-11-18** · cell biology
- why: De novo-designed miniprotein targeting a coiled-coil regulatory surface on kinesin-1, demonstrating a novel approach to modulating motor-MAP interactions.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.16.767073
- abstract: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

## 18. Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
- **2026-11-18** · microbiology
- why: Benchmarks ML methods for antimicrobial peptide prediction and applies them to ancient metagenomes, expanding the search space for novel AMPs.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, ultra large virtual screening
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.17.767431
- abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

## 19. Investigating the critical role of serine in antimicrobial peptide binding to lipopolysaccharide
- **2026-11-19** · biophysics
- why: Uses MD simulations to study antimicrobial peptide binding to LPS, providing atomic-level insights for designing anti-endotoxin therapeutics.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.18.767556
- abstract: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, is a potent endotoxin responsible for triggering severe host immune responses and sepsis. Understanding the atomic-level mechanisms governing how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) recognize and neutralize LPS is essential for designing effective anti-endotoxin therapeutics. Here, we present an in silico investigation of the single-molecule interaction between Escherichia coli O111:B4 LPS and the cationic antimicrobial peptide GL13K, alongside two single-point mutants at position 9 (GL13KS9A and GL13KS9T), using all-atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Consistent with experimental trends, mutating SER9 into alanine significantly alters peptide binding affinity to LPS. Surpisingly, removal of the polar character of serine leads to substantial changes in the interaction of the N-terminus with LPS via the loss of hydrogen bonding to stabilize a hook shape at the C-terminal end. In specific, while wild-type GL13K exhibits the strongest unbinding free-energy barrier, the S9A substitution changes the conformational landscape in such a way as to redirect the peptide's N-terminus from lipid A toward the core oligosaccharide and substantially reduces the unbinding barrier, whereas S9T maintains an similar affinity. Our work demonstrates the effects of distal mutations even in peptides on their binding and lays important groundwork for the development of peptide-based LPS inhibitors.

## 20. Targeting host eIF4A with zotatifin inhibits Bundibugyo virus and other filoviruses
- **2026-11-19** · microbiology
- why: Repurposes a clinical-stage eIF4A inhibitor as a host-directed antiviral against filoviruses, demonstrating a molecular glue mechanism.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.18.767653
- abstract: Filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, depend on host eIF4A helicase activity for replication. Zotatifin is a first in class, clinical stage eIF4A inhibitor that acts as a molecular glue, stabilizing the interaction between eIF4A and selected polypurine rich RNA sequences, thereby inhibiting RNA unwinding and ribosomal scanning. Here, we identify pronounced polypurine enrichment in the 5'untranslated regions (5'UTRs) of the seven major filoviral protein-coding genes NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L across four virus species, including Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Consistent with these findings, zotatifin inhibits the replication of Ebola, Marburg, Sudan, Tai Forest, and Bundibugyo viruses at low nanomolar concentrations. Zotatifin has been administered to humans in oncology and COVID19 clinical studies. Clinical pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling indicates that exposures resulting in inhibition of BDBV replication are achievable in humans at tolerated doses following subcutaneous administration. Together, these findings support the repurposing of zotatifin as a host directed antiviral candidate against BDBV and other filoviruses, with potential applications in preparedness for future outbreaks.
